title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. In E420 (Novi Commentarii 16, 1771/1772) Euler re-founds the calculus of variations by embedding the unknown function in a one-parameter family. For the two-variable part, z = z(x,y,t), and the variation of z is dt(dz/dt). The functional is a double integral ∬V dx dy. V depends on x, y, z and the partial derivatives of z up to third order, with

dV = N dz + P dz_x + P' dz_y + Q dz_xx + Q' dz_xy + Q'' dz_yy + R dz_xxx + R' dz_xxy + R'' dz_xyy + R''' dz_yyy + …

Differentiating ∬V dx dy under the integral sign with respect to t gives ten 'membra' of the form ∬(coefficient)·(∂/∂t of a derivative of z) dx dy. On the previous pages each of these is reduced by repeated integration by parts, in x or in y, to a double integral of z_t times a derivative of the coefficient, plus single integrals.

On this page (§29) the pieces are summed. The variation equals two parts.

First part (double integral):
dt ∬ dx dy z_t [N − P_x − P'_y + Q_xx + Q'_xy + Q''_yy − R_xxx − R'_xxy − R''_xyy − R'''_yyy + …]
The bracket is exactly the Euler–Lagrange (Euler–Ostrogradsky) operator for a third-order Lagrangian in two independent variables. Its alternating signs follow the derivative order and its pattern is that of the mixed-partial lattice; Euler arranges it as a triangle.

Second part: dt times a collection of single integrals. These are the boundary contributions, e.g.
- ∫z_t P dy and ∫z_t P' dx;
- ∫Q z_xt dy − ∫Q_x z_t dy;
- ∫R z_xxt dy − ∫R_x z_xt dy + ∫R_xx z_t dy;
- and so on.
Euler leaves them with indeterminate measure and no stated evaluation points.

§30: Euler confesses that the proper meaning and use of these single-integral members 'cannot yet be perceived at all'. He judges the subject, 'whose first foundations have hardly been laid', to require the attention of all geometers. He adds that even the one-variable theory is not yet clearly understood, and so turns, on the next page, to 'Dilucidationes' for one independent variable.

Purpose: this is the general first-variation formula for multiple-integral problems, e.g. minimal surfaces or plates/membranes, in Euler's new parametric method.
errors:
In the R' and R'' boundary terms the integration-by-parts bookkeeping is inconsistent: the measure (dx vs dy) does not match the mixed derivative of z that appears.
- For R' z_xxy one consistent reduction is ∫R'z_xyt dy − ∫R'_x z_xt dx + ∫R'_xy z_t dy − ∬R'_xxy z_t. Euler writes −∫dy R'_x z_xt.
- For R'' z_xyy, Euler's −∫dx R''_y z_yt should carry dy (or z_xt with dx).
The double-integral (Euler–Lagrange) part is unaffected. These slips are inherited from p.52.

The single integrals are written without specifying the boundary (limits/values of the other variable) at which they are evaluated. For a general domain they are really line integrals around the boundary curve. Euler's formula therefore does not yet constitute a well-defined statement of natural boundary conditions, which is exactly the gap he admits in §30.
The term ∫Q' dy z_yt is correct as written, though it looks inconsistent at first sight. The derivative of Q' that appears with dx is also correct.

ideas.what: Variation of a double integral with Lagrangian depending on partial derivatives up to third order, via a family parameter t; Euler–Lagrange operator with alternating mixed partial derivatives
ideas.modern_name: First variation / Euler–Ostrogradsky equation for higher-order multiple-integral functionals
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760–61, Misc. Taurinensia, minimal surfaces), Euler (E420, 1772); general form Ostrogradsky (1834/38), Poisson
ideas.where_published: E420 itself; related double-integral variations in Euler's Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385/E387 area)

ideas.what: Boundary single-integral terms arising from integration by parts in two variables, left uninterpreted
ideas.modern_name: Boundary terms / natural boundary conditions via the divergence (Green) theorem
ideas.where_published: E420 §§27–30; discussed in Goldstine, A History of the Calculus of Variations (1980), and Fraser's studies of Euler/Lagrange variational calculus

ideas.what: Explicit admission that the meaning of the boundary members is unknown and the multivariable theory is barely founded
ideas.modern_name: Open problem of boundary conditions in multidimensional variational calculus

deep.surprise_reason: The page collects a routine integration-by-parts result: the third-order Euler–Ostrogradsky operator plus boundary terms. Euler's admitted inability to interpret the boundary terms is a known episode in histories of the multivariable calculus of variations, resolved by Gauss, Poisson and Ostrogradsky. The only extra detail is a few bookkeeping slips in the boundary terms.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image essentially; the dx/dy slips in the R', R'' boundary terms (−∫dy(dR'/dx)(ddz/dxdt), −∫dx(dR''/dy)(ddz/dydt)) are in the original print, not transcription errors.
Page header 'VARIATIONVM TRACTANDI. 53' and signature 'G 3' confirmed.
